What the 
testing
 supports
The tests show a measurable Joule–Thomson cooling effect, but downstream hose length erodes the temperature drop. 
Locating the main throttle close to the outlet preserves more cooling.
Further enthalpy reduction should be evaluated. 
Nozzle geometry and fan-assisted flow spreading will determine how effectively the cooled air reaches the target distance.

Two ways to reduce delivered-air enthalpy
Vortex separation is purchasable now; a turboexpander is more efficient in principle but requires a custom matched system
03
1 · VORTEX TUBE
Cold / hot stream separation
No shaft work
The inlet enthalpy is redistributed: a low-enthalpy cold fraction is delivered while a hotter fraction is rejected.
Advantages
•
No moving parts; compact and immediately testable.
•
EXAIR 3208 reference: 6.9 bar(g), 227 SLPM.
Limitations
•
Rejects a hot stream and consumes substantial compressed air.
•
Needs clean, dry air; outlet temperature depends on cold fraction and inlet state.

2 · TURBOEXPANDER
Near-isentropic expansion
Shaft work is extracted
The expanding gas drives a rotor or generator, reducing total enthalpy and total temperature across the whole flow.
Advantages
•
Potentially higher thermodynamic effectiveness; all outlet flow can be cold.
•
Can recover mechanical or electrical work.
Limitations
•
Requires a matched pressure–flow map, load, bearings and overspeed control.
•
Condensation and multistage pressure letdown may require engineered auxiliaries.
